name: Leader election in programmable matter

origin.note: Introduced with shape formation at DNA 21 (2015).

related.relation: Both elect a leader among anonymous entities from geometry alone; particles on the lattice can also move and talk to neighbours, robots in the plane only see [Dufoulon2021Efficient].

summary: Anonymous constant-memory particles must elect exactly one leader, which most shape-formation algorithms need first.
statement: A connected **configuration** (the set of nodes occupied by particles) of $n$ anonymous particles (initially contracted) must reach a state in which exactly one particle is the leader and all others know they are not. **Time** is in asynchronous rounds; $L_{out}$ is the length of the outer boundary and $D$ the diameter of the configuration.

primer.intro: Imagine a swarm of identical tiny machines, packed together on a floor tiled with triangles, that must pick one boss without any name tags. Each machine is a **particle**. It occupies one **node** of the **triangular lattice**, the infinite tiling of the plane by equilateral triangles whose corners are the nodes; particles on adjacent nodes are **neighbours**. A particle remembers only a few bits, and can read and write the memory of its neighbours. It moves in two steps: an **expansion** into an empty adjacent node, after which it briefly occupies both nodes, then a **contraction** into one of the two; so one expansion and one contraction move it by one node. In the standard version there are $n$ particles whose nodes form one connected **configuration**, possibly with **holes** (empty regions enclosed by particles); all particles agree on what clockwise means (**chirality**), but not on a common north. An adversary, a scheduler that we assume chooses the worst order, decides when each particle acts; each time a particle acts is an **activation**, and a **round** is a stretch of time in which every particle has been activated at least once. The goal: exactly one particle ends in state **leader**, every other particle knows it is not, and we count the rounds this takes.

ideas.title: Erosion: peel the configuration from the outside
ideas.idea:
This works on configurations **without holes**. It is the erosion of [DiLuna2020Shape], which [DAngelo2020Silent] showed can be run even by particles with no memory and no messages. No particle changes its node (in the memoryless version, expansions serve as signals).

1. Every particle starts as *eligible*.
2. An eligible particle is a *corner* if its eligible neighbours are few and sit next to each other: none, one, two that are neighbours of each other, or three in a row.
3. A corner drops out (becomes ineligible). Corners keep dropping out round after round, so the configuration is eaten from its outer **boundary** (the particles next to the empty outside; a hole has a boundary too) inwards, like a coastline eroded by the sea.
4. A few special cases stop the peeling: a lone eligible particle, two eligible particles that are each other's only eligible neighbour, or a triangle of three, become **candidates** (for leader) instead of dropping out.
5. At the end, 1, 2 or 3 candidates remain, each a neighbour of the others.
ideas.analysis: A hole-free configuration always has a corner, and removing corners never splits the eligible particles into parts or creates a hole, so erosion never gets stuck. Each removal leaves fewer eligible particles, and [DAngelo2020Silent] show the process ends in $O(n)$ rounds. It cannot always leave a single leader: three particles in a triangle look exactly alike (see the next idea). It also fails with holes: in a ring of particles around a hole, each particle has two eligible neighbours that are not neighbours of each other, so nobody is a corner. The best known result elects exactly one leader, holes allowed, deterministically in $O(L_{out}+D)$ rounds, where $L_{out}$ is the length of the outer boundary and $D$ the diameter of the configuration [Dufoulon2021Efficient].
ideas.why_it_matters: Erosion is the first step of the deterministic shape-formation algorithm and is reused whenever a few candidate leaders are good enough.

ideas.title: Three identical particles in a triangle
ideas.idea: Take three particles forming a small triangle, and suppose particles never move and the scheduler may activate all three at the same moment. Each particle sees the same picture: two neighbours, one to its left and one to its right (they have chirality, so 'left' means the same to all). They start in the same state, so in their first activation they compute the same thing and write the same thing. After that activation they are again in identical states with identical views, and so on forever. Whatever a deterministic algorithm (one that flips no coins) does, either all three become leader or none does [Chalopin2026Stationary].
ideas.analysis: The argument only uses symmetry: an algorithm cannot tell apart particles whose surroundings are rotated copies of each other. The same reasoning shows that a configuration with six-fold symmetry may end with six leaders, which is why stationary particles with chirality elect up to six leaders [Bazzi2019Stationary]. To get exactly one leader, papers add something that breaks the symmetry: coin flips [Derakhshandeh2015Leader], a scheduler that activates one particle at a time [Briones2023Asynchronous], or a common direction [Chalopin2026Stationary].
ideas.why_it_matters: Symmetry is the basic obstacle in all of programmable matter; it explains why results say 'at most three' or 'at most six' leaders.

ideas.title: Coin flips along the boundaries
ideas.idea:
Only particles on a boundary (the outer boundary, or the boundary of a hole) take part. Each boundary closes on itself, and with chirality everyone walks it in the same direction.

1. Every boundary particle starts as a candidate. Between two consecutive candidates lies a *segment* of non-candidates.
2. Compare segments: a candidate whose segment ahead is shorter than the segment behind it gives up (particles compare lengths by passing tokens, one per particle).
3. If all segments are equal, every candidate flips a coin. On heads it passes its candidacy forward to the next candidate's spot; when it does and the next candidate keeps its own, two candidacies land on one spot and merge.
4. A candidate that is alone on its boundary checks whether it is the outer boundary (by adding up the turns along it; the outer boundary turns one full circle one way, the boundary of a hole the other way). Alone on the outer boundary: it is the leader. Alone on the boundary of a hole: it gives up.
ideas.analysis: There is always at least one candidate on the outer boundary, and while there are two or more, each phase removes one with probability at least $1/4$, so the number of candidates keeps shrinking. Holes are no problem, because the boundary of a hole eventually loses all its candidates. The expected time is $O(L_{max})$ rounds, $L_{max}$ the length of the longest boundary [Derakhshandeh2015Leader]; this was improved to $O(n)$ rounds with high probability [Daymude2017Improved], and later matched without coins [Dufoulon2021Efficient].
ideas.why_it_matters: Working on boundaries instead of the whole configuration is the idea behind the fast algorithms that followed.

glossary.definition: an anonymous entity with constant memory that occupies one node of the triangular lattice (contracted) or two adjacent nodes (expanded), and reads and writes only its own memory and its neighbours'
the infinite graph whose nodes are the corners of the tiling of the plane by equilateral triangles; each node has six adjacent nodes
a point of the triangular lattice; a contracted particle occupies one node, an expanded particle two adjacent nodes
a particle that occupies a node adjacent to a node of the given particle
the set of nodes occupied by the particles; it is connected when every particle can be reached from every other through neighbours
the move in which a contracted particle extends into an empty adjacent node and then occupies both nodes
the move in which an expanded particle withdraws into one of its two nodes
a finite connected set of empty nodes enclosed by the configuration

the closed sequence of particles adjacent to one connected region of empty nodes: the outer boundary (towards the infinite empty region, of length $L_{out}$) or the boundary of a hole; $L_{max}$ is the length of the longest boundary
a common sense of clockwise shared by all particles (but no common north)
one step of a particle, at a time chosen by the scheduler: it reads its memory and its neighbours', computes, writes, and may perform one expansion or contraction
an asynchronous round: an interval of time in which every particle is activated at least once; a bound holds for every division of the execution into consecutive rounds
a particle that may still become the leader; erosion ends with 1, 2 or 3 candidates, each a neighbour of the others
the one particle that ends in state leader; every other particle ends knowing that it is not the leader

history: Leader election was the first task studied, because shape formation needs a leader [Derakhshandeh2015Leader]. The first question was **feasibility with constant memory**, then **rounds**: randomized algorithms came first [Derakhshandeh2015Leader] [Daymude2017Improved], then deterministic ones without chirality [Emek2019Deterministic] and in linear time [Dufoulon2021Efficient]. Later work weakened the model in three directions: **stationary** particles [Bazzi2019Stationary] [Chalopin2026Stationary], **asynchronous** adversaries [Briones2023Asynchronous], and **silent, oblivious** particles [DAngelo2020Silent]; self-stabilising election with constant memory followed [Chalopin2025SelfStab] [Chalopin2026Holes].

variants.title: Deterministic, with chirality
variants.summary: Deterministic leader election in $O(L_{out}+D)$ rounds, as fast as the best randomized algorithm, holes allowed.

results.note: Introductory for linear time and current best; $O(D_A)$, where $D_A$ is the diameter of the area enclosed by the particles (holes included), if particles know whether their boundary is the outer one. The system may temporarily disconnect.

time.note: Only an informal $\Omega(D)$ remark; no proven lower bound.

open: Fast deterministic leader election under weaker (non-atomic) schedulers, and without letting the system disconnect [Dufoulon2021Efficient].

variants.title: Randomized, with chirality
variants.summary: Randomized leader election in a linear number of rounds with high probability.

results.note: Expected rounds; $L_{max}$ is the longest boundary.
With high probability; restated as $O(L_{out}+D)$ by [Dufoulon2021Efficient].

variants.notes: In the general amoebot model on arbitrary graphs leader election is impossible, by reduction to anonymous rings [Derakhshandeh2015Leader].

variants.title: Deterministic, no orientation
variants.summary: Without chirality, a unique leader can still be elected deterministically, in $O(L_{out}n^2)$ rounds.

results.note: Introductory and current best; also yields agreement on chirality.

time.note: Far from the linear bound known with chirality.

open: Deterministic leader election without chirality in linear time.

variants.title: Silent oblivious particles (SILBOT)
variants.summary: Silent oblivious particles (SILBOT) elect at most three mutually adjacent leaders from hole-free configurations in $O(n)$ rounds.

assumes: initial configuration deeply simply connected (e.g. all particles contracted, no holes)
results.note: Introductory and current best: Algorithm LESC (Theorem 1), which only expands particles; an emulation of the erosion of [DiLuna2020Shape] with simpler rules.

variants.notes: SILBOT [DAngelo2020Silent] removes from the amoebot model the serialised scheduler (no two neighbouring particles active together), explicit communication, atomicity of actions and randomness. Particles see up to two hops, distinguish empty nodes from contracted and expanded particles, and act asynchronously; a particle that has expanded along an edge is committed and contracts into the target node at its next activation if the node is empty. A round is the shortest period in which every particle has completed an activation. The paper argues that 1-hop visibility is not enough without communication. Holes are handled in the variant without the hole-free assumption. Checked against the full text of [DAngelo2020Silent] (IEEE Access version; preliminary version at AAMAS 2020).
variants.statement: Particle leader election (PLE): from a connected configuration of contracted particles, terminate with one, two or three mutually adjacent contracted particles that recognise themselves as LEADER, every other particle expanded (NON-LEADER), and the system connected throughout. A single leader is not required: D'Angelo et al. note that a single particle can be elected only with randomisation or a sequential scheduler, citing [Emek2019Deterministic].

variants.title: SILBOT with holes
variants.summary: With holes, SILBOT particles cannot elect up to three leaders while staying connected; if they can tell a hole from the exterior, election with compaction takes $O(n^2)$ rounds.
variants.statement: Particle leader election as in the hole-free SILBOT variant (one, two or three mutually adjacent leaders), from any connected configuration of contracted particles, possibly with holes, keeping the system connected.

preconditions: a connected configuration with a hole in which groups of particles have identical 2-hop views
the adversary activates each such set simultaneously, each particle twice in a row
holds even with unlimited memory and chirality
lower_bounds.note: Theorem 2: every move some particle could be instructed to make disconnects the system under some schedule.

assumes: exterior awareness: a particle tells an empty node in a hole from an exterior empty node within its view
results.note: Introductory and current best: Algorithm CHLE (Theorem 3) fills the holes (compaction: the configuration becomes simply connected) while electing at most three leaders; on hole-free configurations it behaves as LESC.

time.note: Impossible in plain SILBOT; with exterior awareness $O(n^2)$ rounds and no lower bound.

open: Can SILBOT particles elect leaders from configurations with holes if the system may disconnect temporarily, without exterior awareness? The impossibility of [DAngelo2020Silent] assumes that connectivity is preserved.
variants.notes: *Compaction* (of holes) asks to turn any connected configuration into a simply connected one. Exterior awareness is motivated by local sensing (light or pressure). Checked against the full text of [DAngelo2020Silent].

variants.title: Stationary, chirality, no holes
variants.summary: On hole-free configurations with chirality, stationary constant-memory particles elect a leader deterministically in $O(n)$ rounds.

results.note: Introductory and current best: $O(r + m_{tree})$ rounds, fewer than $2n$ (Proposition 1). Also computes k-local identifiers; works on the square, triangular and king grids.

variants.notes: $r$ and $m_{tree}$ are parameters of the configuration defined in [Gastineau2019Leader]: $r$ is the radius of the configuration with respect to its border particles (the least, over particles $u$, of the largest distance from $u$ to a border particle), and $m_{tree}$ is the largest height of an induced subgraph of the configuration that is a tree. The scheduler is strong, as listed by [Dufoulon2021Efficient]. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Stationary, chirality, weak scheduler
variants.statement: Up to six leaders may be elected.
variants.summary: Without moving, particles with chirality elect at most six leaders in $O(n^2)$ rounds, holes allowed.

results.note: Introductory and current best; at most six leaders.

open: Is a unique leader ever impossible for stationary particles with chirality? Dufoulon et al. say this was shown in [Bazzi2019Stationary], at least for a weak scheduler [Dufoulon2021Efficient]; the theorem was not read.
variants.notes: Bounds are from the table of Dufoulon, Kutten and Moses [Dufoulon2021Efficient]; the abstract of [Bazzi2019Stationary] was not read.

variants.title: Stationary, common direction, no chirality
variants.summary: With one common direction and no chirality, a unique leader is elected without moving, with obstacles allowed, but only with implicit termination.

preconditions: holds even under a synchronous scheduler

results.note: Introductory and current best (Section 6); implicit termination, unique leader, deterministic, stationary.

variants.notes: With chirality but no common direction, explicit termination is always possible but the number of leaders depends on the symmetry of the initial configuration [Chalopin2026Stationary]. Here "common direction" means agreement on one axis only. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Stationary, asynchronous, no orientation, no holes
variants.summary: Stationary particles with no common orientation elect a leader in connected, contractible 2D or 3D systems under an unfair asynchronous adversary; the running time there is not analysed.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Corollary 6): the sequential algorithm transformed by the concurrency control framework [Daymude2023Canonical]; the paper says its runtime "has not yet been analyzed".

time.note: Runtime not analysed under the asynchronous adversary.

open: Deterministic leader election in $O(L_{out}+D)$ rounds under a weaker scheduler [Dufoulon2021Efficient].
variants.notes: Contractible means no holes, in 2D or in 3D (face-centred cubic lattice). Particles have "assorted orientations": no common direction and no chirality. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Oblivious, common compass, holes allowed
variants.summary: Oblivious particles that agree on all directions elect a unique leader in connected configurations with holes, self-stabilising, using movement, under an unfair sequential scheduler.

assumes: unfair sequential scheduler with atomic moves
results.note: Introductory and current best; silent self-stabilising.

variants.notes: The abstract says "common sense of direction"; Section 2 assumes agreement on all directions. Movement together with this orientation overcomes the impossibility of constant-memory self-stabilising election in general networks [Chalopin2026Holes]. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Stationary, sequential, no orientation, no holes
variants.summary: Under an unfair sequential adversary, stationary particles with no common orientation elect a unique leader in $O(n)$ rounds, in 2D or 3D.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3 and Corollary 4).

variants.title: Stationary, fair scheduler, no orientation, no holes
variants.summary: Stationary constant-memory particles with no orientation and no chirality elect a unique leader from any initial memory: silent self-stabilising election on simply connected systems.

results.note: Introductory and current best. The algorithm fails under an unfair scheduler (Section 6). Constant memory suffices although silent self-stabilising election in general networks needs $\Omega(\log n)$ bits, even on rings.

variants.notes: Self-stabilisation is a stronger requirement than the problem statement and has no axis here. Checked against the full text.

axes.name: Movement

values.label: stationary: particles never move
values.definition: No particle ever expands or contracts; the configuration is fixed and only states change.

values.label: particles may move
values.definition: Particles may expand and contract during the election.

axes.origin: The early leader-election algorithms for amoebots only exchanged messages, and "did not use the movement ability as an aid to the computation" [Dufoulon2021Efficient]. Emek et al. showed that movement lets particles elect a unique leader deterministically with no assumption on chirality or holes; the main idea is "the usage of the ability of the amoebots to move, which previous leader election algorithms have not used" [Emek2019Deterministic]. The stationary setting stayed interesting because particles may be unable to move, "so as to maintain a configuration or due to the presence of obstacles" [Chalopin2026Stationary]. Bazzi and Briones studied stationary deterministic election [Bazzi2019Stationary], where symmetric configurations can force up to six leaders (as reported by [Dufoulon2021Efficient]). Chalopin, Das and Kokkou showed that one common direction suffices for a unique stationary leader [Chalopin2026Stationary].

figure.caption: Leader election by erosion on a configuration without holes: no particle moves. An eligible particle (blue) whose eligible neighbours are few and consecutive (none, one, two that are neighbours of each other, three in a row) is a corner and drops out (grey); corners drop out round after round, peeling the configuration from its boundary, until a single candidate remains and becomes the leader [DiLuna2020Shape] [DAngelo2020Silent]. Configurations with holes need other algorithms [Derakhshandeh2015Leader].

frames.label: Final: one candidate left, the leader
